c.st: ‘Mind blowing’ ancient settlements uncovered in the Amazon
c.x: 1491 by Michael Mann is a must read for anyone even vaguely interested in the Americas before European arrival. It’s a fantastic book that will change how you think about indigenous cultures in the Americas and make this kind of thing seem a lot less surprising.

c.st: Beyond Greece and Rome
c.x:
…been improving of late), but for what it's worth, my favorite book on history "beyond Greece and Rome" so far has been Charles C. Mann's 1491. In fact, it's one of the best and most illuminating books I've read, period.

It has about the information/idea density of a Neal Stephenson novel (a good one), and is about equally a pageturner.

I've also adored all of Jimmy Maher's (better known as The Digital Antiquarian) amateur history books, his Wonders of the World series - I think the one on Chinese history was…

c.st: Archaeologists discover tomb of first king of Caracol
c.x: Shout-out again to Charles C. Mann's excellent book 1491. One of my most eye-opening reads after 2000, in terms of information that I didn't possess yet, exceedingly well presented.

c.st: Why books don't work (2019)
c.x: I always recommend Charles Mann's 1491 as the antidote to Guns, Germs, and Steel. (Although note that this focuses entirely on pre-Columbian America.)

c.st: Ask HN: Which book do you keep asking people to read?
c.x:
Nabokov ends one of the most captivating fragments of Pale Fire with a sentence "I trust the reader has enjoyed this note."

He totally got me.

It is not the book I would recommend most often, it just came to my mind.

What I would recommend the most are psychological books. 'Mind and Nature' by Gregory Bateson is one of my favorites.

Posts like this one are awesome, always happy to sieve through.

c.st: Bateson and Me – Part 1 (2004)
c.x:
Funny. I started writing

"...Bateson (and Korzybski) are one of mostly undervalued thinkers in my opinion..."

Bateson's "Mind and Nature" and Korzybski's "Science and Sanity" make a good, eye opening read.

c.st: Book Review: Rhythms of the Brain
c.x:
I strongly recommend his next book, "The Brain From Inside Out". While Rhythms of the Brain is indeed aimed at neuroscientists, and is pretty heavy reading, Inside Out seems to be from more of a hacker's perspective.

They're good compliments to each other, but I found Inside Out to be a bit more actionable.
